**Viscosity can dissipate energy at every instant while a velocity disturbance grows.** Growth is possible when the disturbance receives energy from a background shear faster than viscosity removes it. As the shear changes the wave's orientation and wavelength, that balance changes too.

This is the dynamical question behind the [previous article's oscillating velocities](../d4_mean_stress/article.html). We showed that zero-mean motion can carry momentum. But prescribing an oscillation does not explain where its energy comes from, how its stress evolves, or why its lifetime might be limited.

The proposed OpenAI construction uses pulses whose growth draws on the background shear and whose later decay involves viscosity. Its pulse amplitude equation retains viscous damping explicitly. [OpenAI, Section 2.2 and Equation (7.22)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/32d9f210-8b73-45e0-91bc-82a30aef8a9a/navier-stokes.pdf)

We will study an explicit two-dimensional example called a *Kelvin shearing wave*. It is simple enough to derive, evaluate, and check against an independent time integrator. We will track its velocity, wavelength, momentum covariance, and energy budget together. This is a reduced illustration of growth and decay; it does not reconstruct the paper's rotating, localized pulse.

## Start with a shear that tilts a pattern

Take a background velocity

$$
\mathbf U=(Sy,0).
$$

Fluid at larger $y$ moves faster in the horizontal direction. A stripe painted across the flow therefore tilts: its upper portion moves farther than its lower portion.

For a wave with phase

$$
\phi(x,y,t)=k_xx+k_y(t)y,
$$

transport by the background requires

$$
k_y(t)=k_{y0}-Sk_xt.
$$

Indeed, $\partial_t\phi+Sy\,\partial_x\phi=0$. The phase moves with the background even though its wavevector changes.

We use $S=1$, $k_x=1$, and $k_{y0}=4$, all dimensionless. At $t=4$, $k_y$ passes through zero. Before that instant the wavevector gets shorter and the distance between wave crests grows. Afterward its length increases and the crests crowd together.

The wavelength measured perpendicular to the crests is

$$
\lambda(t)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y(t)^2}}.
$$

This is a wavelength in the laboratory coordinates, not a fixed wavelength in a coordinate system that moves with the shear. To assign a dimensional length, multiply it by the chosen reference length $L_{\rm ref}$. No fluid-specific reference length is assigned here.

## One wave can be solved exactly

Write the perturbation vorticity as

$$
\omega'(x,y,t)=\zeta(t)\cos\phi.
$$

The corresponding incompressible velocity is

$$
\mathbf w(x,y,t)=\mathbf B(t)\sin\phi,\qquad
\mathbf B(t)=\frac{\zeta(t)}{K^2(t)}
\binom{-k_y(t)}{k_x},\qquad K^2=k_x^2+k_y^2.
$$

The velocity points along the wave crests, perpendicular to the wavevector. This gives $\nabla\cdot\mathbf w=0$ and also makes its self-advection $(\mathbf w\cdot\nabla)\mathbf w$ vanish. The two-dimensional background vorticity is constant, so the perturbation vorticity obeys

$$
\zeta'=-\nu K^2(t)\zeta.
$$

Its exact solution is

$$
\zeta(t)=\zeta_0e^{-\nu I(t)},
\qquad
I(t)=
(k_x^2+k_{y0}^2)t
-Sk_xk_{y0}t^2
+\frac{S^2k_x^2}{3}t^3.
$$

The integral $I(t)=\int_0^tK^2(s)\,ds$ records the accumulated effect of diffusion. The cubic term matters at late times because the shear makes $|k_y|$ grow approximately linearly.

This is the two-dimensional specialization of a classical exact shearing-wave family; our axes are interchanged relative to the reference's background shear. [Singh and Sridhar, Equations (1)–(7)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1101.5507v2)

The peak perturbation speed is

$$
U_{\rm wave}(t)=|\mathbf B(t)|=\frac{|\zeta(t)|}{K(t)}.
$$

Vorticity decreases under viscosity, but velocity also depends on the changing wavevector. While $K$ decreases, velocity can increase even though $\zeta$ decreases.

Choose viscosity $\nu=0.005$ and an initial peak wave speed of one. In this example, the speed reaches **`{python} f'{summary["peak_speed_ratio"]:.2f}'` times its initial value** near $t=\,$**`{python} f'{summary["peak_time"]:.3f}'`**. Its phase-averaged kinetic energy increases by approximately **`{python} f'{summary["peak_energy_ratio"]:.1f}'` times**.

The heat-equation reference uses the same initial perturbation and viscosity, with zero background shear. Its wavevector remains fixed, so its speed decays exponentially from the beginning. A second reference keeps the shear and sets viscosity to zero, isolating the geometric amplification.

At $t=20$, the speed is only **`{python} f'{summary["final_speed_ratio"]:.3g}'` of its initial value**. There is no singularity: this example has a finite transient peak followed by decay.

## The energy budget says where growth comes from

Average over one wave phase. The perturbation kinetic energy per unit mass is

$$
E=\frac12\langle|\mathbf w|^2\rangle=\frac{|\mathbf B|^2}{4},
$$

and the momentum covariance is

$$
Q_{xy}=\langle w_xw_y\rangle=\frac{B_xB_y}{2}.
$$

Differentiating the exact solution gives

$$
\boxed{\frac{dE}{dt}=
\underbrace{-S Q_{xy}}_{\text{shear production}}
-\underbrace{2\nu K^2E}_{\text{viscous dissipation}}.}
$$

Initially $Q_{xy}<0$, so $-SQ_{xy}>0$: the shear-production term supplies perturbation energy. Viscosity still removes energy. Growth occurs when production exceeds that loss.

The same statement in terms of speed is

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\log U_{\rm wave}
=\frac{Sk_xk_y}{K^2}-\nu K^2.
$$

At the speed peak these terms balance. Viscosity moves the peak slightly before the geometric turning time $t=4$. After $k_y$ becomes negative, the production term also becomes negative. Both shear exchange and viscosity then decrease the perturbation energy.

This particular wave has a spatially uniform phase-averaged covariance. Its stress divergence is zero, so it does not provide the spatially varying mean force demonstrated in D4. The affine background is unbounded and has no finite whole-space energy. Its shear-production budget must not be interpreted as a closed, finite fluid reservoir or a finite-energy blowup construction.

## Check the dynamics independently

The analytic solution generates the article's curves. To test it independently, we integrate the projected momentum equation for the two velocity amplitudes:

$$
\mathbf B'
=-SB_y\binom{1}{0}
+\frac{2Sk_xB_y}{K^2}\binom{k_x}{k_y}
-\nu K^2\mathbf B.
$$

The middle term comes from the pressure required to preserve incompressibility as the wavevector turns. We use classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta, without projecting away any numerical divergence error.

![Halving the time step reduces the independent amplitude error approximately as a fourth-order method predicts. The second panel compares accumulated damping for a changing wavevector with damping at the fixed initial wavevector. Early wavelength growth reduces damping relative to the fixed-wavevector reference; later wavelength shortening strengthens it.](figures/03_time_accuracy_and_damping.png){#fig-accuracy fig-alt="The RK4 amplitude error decreases at fourth order, and the sheared-wave damping eventually overtakes the fixed-wavevector reference."}

The plotted histories have spacing $\Delta t=0.01$. The independent refinement study uses steps from $0.4$ down to $0.025$; at the finest step, its largest vector-amplitude error is approximately **`{python} f'{summary["finest_rk4_amplitude_error"]:.2g}'`**. This is an error against the analytic solution, not an estimate from comparing two equally uncertain simulations.

Further checks differentiate the velocity and pressure in physical space and time, substitute them into the primitive momentum equation, verify the phase-averaged stress, and integrate the energy budget. ## What carries over to the paper's pulses?

The example connects three observable quantities: wave orientation controls wavelength, momentum covariance controls shear production, and accumulated squared wavenumber controls viscous attenuation.

The OpenAI pulse construction additionally uses rotating and axial shear, localized envelopes, two admissible flux families, seeding, and corrections. Our two-dimensional transient growth is a different mechanism from that complete construction; its initial wavelength lengthens before shortening. [OpenAI, Sections 7.2–7.3](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/32d9f210-8b73-45e0-91bc-82a30aef8a9a/navier-stokes.pdf)

There is no small parameter or source calibration here that turns this Kelvin wave into the paper's actual pulse. It is a fully specified example that explains why “viscosity is dissipative” does not imply “every disturbance decays monotonically.”

The [notebook](../../code/d5_shearing_wave/study.ipynb), [parameters](../../code/d5_shearing_wave/parameters.json), and [CSV data](../../code/d5_shearing_wave/data/) support experiments with different viscosity, shear, and initial orientation. The next deliverable will examine which corrections in the original construction can actually be evaluated and what inputs they require.
